newsitem.title: BURUNDI: U.N. rejects Burundi's request for tribunal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. rejects Burundi's request for tribunal.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has rejected Burundi's request for an international tribunal into the assassination of President Melchior Ndadaye in 1993, the government said on Friday.
The army, meanwhile, said it killed 20 Hutu rebels and set free 3,000 civilians in Bururi province, scene of repeated skirmishes since April.
Foreign Minister Luc Rukingama published Annan's letter dated June 26 rejecting the request and said it posed a grave threat to its peace process.

"The government of...Burundi considers that the position of Kofi Annan in his letter refusing this international tribune presents a grave hinderance to the fight against impunity and against genocidal ideologies and the peace process in Burundi," Rukingama said in a statement.
Ndadaye, Burundi's first freely elected Hutu president, was murdered in an attempted coup by Tutsi troops in October 1993, sparking a civil war in which more than 150,000 people have been killed.

Hutus rose up after Ndadaye's death and killed thousands of minority Tutsis in what an August 1996 U.N. Commission termed "acts of genocide", which were followed by repression from the Tutsi-dominated army.
Burundi's military leader Pierre Buyoya, who took power in a coup last July requested a U.N. tribunal as part of a process aimed at restoring peace.
Annan rejected the request after considering a recommendation given in the Commission's report, which said that "international jurisdiction was not a realistic option".

"The circumstances to which reference was made in the Commission's report have not changed since, not at least in a way which would now justify the establishment of an international jurisdiction," said the letter.
Buyoya in May announced a pre-ceasefire agreement with the main Hutu rebel group, the National Council for the Defence of Democracy.
Since then he has faced stiff opposition from ethnic Tutsis who deem it wrong to talk to a "genocidal" rebel group, and Hutu moderates offended at being sidelined by the agreement.
Buyoya was depending on the U.N. tribunal to bolster his hand against critics, one foreign analyst said.
